words.definition: Real and exactly what it appears to be, not fake.
words.example: The dealer confirmed the painting was a genuine Rembrandt, not a clever copy.
words.mnemonic: Gen-u-ine holds 'gene' — your genes are authentically yours and can't be counterfeited.

words.definition: Behaving in a natural, sincere way without pretense or show.
words.example: Despite her fame, she stayed unaffected, chatting with fans like they were old friends.
words.mnemonic: Un-affected = no 'act' added on — nothing fake layered over the real person.

words.definition: Showing deep, sincere emotion from the core of one's being.
words.example: In a heartfelt speech, he thanked his mother through streaming tears.
words.mnemonic: Break it apart: 'heart' + 'felt' — emotion you literally felt straight in your heart.

words.definition: A false attitude adopted only to impress or mislead others.
words.example: His tough talk was mere posture; he backed down the instant anyone challenged him.
words.mnemonic: Like striking a 'pose' for a camera — a stance you strike purely for show, not for truth.

words.definition: Not honestly meant; pretending to feel emotions you do not truly have.
words.example: Her insincere apology fooled no one; she smirked the whole time she said sorry.
words.mnemonic: In- (not) + sincere — picture a 'sinner' faking a sweet smile he doesn't mean.

words.definition: Behaving in a way that plainly contradicts your claimed beliefs.
words.example: It was hypocritical of her to ban sweets while eating cake in secret.
words.mnemonic: Spot the 'critic' inside it — someone who criticizes others for exactly what he secretly does.

words.definition: Dishonest and deliberately misleading in order to hide the truth.
words.example: The deceitful salesman hid the car's flood damage under a fresh coat of paint.
words.mnemonic: De-CEIT sounds like 'the cheat' — a cheat who lies to your face.

words.definition: To trick or confuse someone, usually by cheating them.
words.example: The street hustler bamboozled tourists with a rigged shell game.
words.mnemonic: 'Bamboo' + 'zle' — imagine being bonked dizzy with a bamboo stick until you're confused and fleeced.

words.definition: Deceptive nonsense or empty pretense meant to mislead people.
words.example: "Christmas? Bah, humbug!" Scrooge scoffed, dismissing it as sentimental rubbish.
words.mnemonic: 'Hum' + 'bug' — a bug that just hums fake noise, all sound and no substance.

words.definition: Exaggerated and showy, as if performing on a stage.
words.example: With a theatrical sigh, he flung the door open and stormed out of the room.
words.mnemonic: Rooted in 'theater' — imagine every gesture happening under spotlights before an audience.

words.definition: Exaggeratedly and unpleasantly flattering; slick and oily in manner.
words.example: The oleaginous waiter drenched every guest in greasy, over-the-top compliments.
words.mnemonic: 'Oleo' means oil (as in oleo-margarine) — picture a slick, greasy, too-smooth smile.

words.definition: Excessive praise offered to please someone or gain advantage.
words.example: His constant flattery about her genius was really just a bid for a raise.
words.mnemonic: It 'flatters' — laid on thick like butter spread flat to win someone's favor.

words.definition: To speak or act insincerely, especially by using misleading half-truths to avoid a straight answer.
words.example: The witness would palter and dodge, giving vague replies until the lawyer lost all patience.
words.mnemonic: Sounds like 'falter' — a palterer falters around the truth, wobbling instead of saying it plainly.

words.definition: To attribute a fault, crime, or quality to a person, often without solid proof.
words.example: Critics were quick to impute selfish motives to her charity work.
words.mnemonic: 'Im-' (onto) + Latin 'putare' (to reckon) — to reckon a fault onto someone.

words.definition: To belittle or disparage; to take away from the worth or standing of something.
words.example: He never missed a chance to derogate his colleagues' achievements during meetings.
words.mnemonic: 'De-' (down) + 'rogate' (to ask/propose) — to talk something down, to lower it.

words.definition: Genuine and sincere, not faked or put on for effect.
words.example: Her unfeigned delight at the surprise party brought tears to everyone's eyes.
words.mnemonic: 'Un-' + 'feigned' (faked) — literally NOT faked, therefore the real thing.

words.definition: A person who argues cleverly but deceptively, using flawed reasoning to appear correct.
words.example: The debate coach warned us never to become a sophist who wins by trickery rather than truth.
words.mnemonic: Sounds like 'so-fist' — punches you with slick arguments; from Greek 'sophos' (wise), cunningly twisted.

words.definition: A person who adopts a false manner or attitude to impress others.
words.example: The café was full of poseurs clutching untouched philosophy books to look intellectual.
words.mnemonic: French for 'one who poses' — strikes a pose for the camera but has no real substance behind it.

words.definition: The practice of using insincere flattery to win favor from powerful people.
words.example: The intern's constant sycophancy toward the boss annoyed everyone else in the office.
words.mnemonic: Say 'sick-o-fancy' — it's sickening how fancy the flattery gets.

words.definition: A feeling of doubt or hesitation about whether an action is morally right.
words.example: She had no scruple about reading her sister's diary while she was out.
words.mnemonic: From Latin 'scrupulus,' a tiny sharp stone in your shoe — a nagging moral pebble.

words.definition: Having no moral principles; willing to be dishonest or unfair in order to succeed.
words.example: The unscrupulous landlord evicted tenants illegally just to raise the rent.
words.mnemonic: A person with NO moral pebbles ([[scruple]]) in their shoe to slow them down.

words.definition: To repeatedly change one's opinions or loyalties; to be deliberately ambiguous.
words.example: Voters tired of a senator who would tergiversate on every issue to please each crowd.
words.mnemonic: 'Tergi' (back) + 'versate' (turn) — turning your back and spinning to face any direction.

words.definition: According to what is stated or appears true, though perhaps not really so.
words.example: He arrived early ostensibly to help, but really to snoop through the files.
words.mnemonic: From Latin 'ostendere' (to show) — what is shown on the surface, while reality hides beneath.

words.definition: A firm, emphatic public declaration that something is or is not true.
words.example: Despite his loud protestations of innocence, the jury had already seen the security video.
words.mnemonic: Hidden 'protest' inside it — a protestation is a strong protest-style declaration.

words.definition: Overly flattering or polite in a way that feels insincere and slick.
words.example: The smarmy salesman complimented her shoes three times before slipping in the warranty upsell.
words.mnemonic: Smarmy = 'smear' + balmy: picture someone smearing oily charm all over you.

words.definition: Excessively sweet or emotional to the point of feeling fake and sickening.
words.example: The greeting card's saccharine verse about guardian angels made her roll her eyes.
words.mnemonic: Saccharin is the artificial sweetener — a saccharine mood is that same fake, sugary overload.

words.definition: The act of closely copying another's speech, behavior, or appearance.
words.example: The parrot's mimicry was so precise it reproduced the exact ringtone of her phone.
words.mnemonic: You can hear 'mimic' inside it — mimicry is simply what a skilled mimic does.

words.definition: A statement or principle that is genuinely true and beyond dispute.
words.example: She clung to one verity through the scandal: honesty outlasts a clever lie.
words.mnemonic: Holds the Latin root 'veri-' (true), the same piece inside 'verify' and 'very'.

words.definition: An open, frank declaration or acknowledgment of something one believes or has done.
words.example: His public avowal of guilt surprised the courtroom, since everyone had expected denial.
words.mnemonic: Hear the 'VOW' in a-VOW-al: a vow spoken aloud for everyone to hear.

words.definition: To declare openly and take responsibility for the truth of a claim.
words.example: I can avouch her honesty, for I have known her well for twenty years.
words.mnemonic: a-VOUCH: to avouch is to vouch for something, staking your own word on it.

words.definition: Genuine and real, exactly what it claims to be, not copied or faked.
words.example: The dealer confirmed the painting was authentic, not a later workshop imitation.
words.mnemonic: Contains 'author' — an authentic work traces straight back to its true author.

words.definition: To deceive someone by pretending confidence, strength, or intentions one does not have.
words.example: Holding a weak hand, he tried to bluff the other players into folding.
words.mnemonic: Picture a poker player puffing his chest at a steep cliff (a 'bluff'), daring you to call.

words.definition: Insincere, hypocritical talk, especially about religion or morality, meant to seem virtuous.
words.example: The politician's speech was pure cant, mouthing virtues he clearly never practiced.
words.mnemonic: Sounds like 'can't' — you can't trust the smooth, holy-sounding talk of a hypocrite.

words.definition: To imitate the appearance or feeling of something in order to deceive or model it.
words.example: The actor could simulate grief so convincingly that the whole audience wept.
words.mnemonic: 'similar' + look: you make something look similar enough to pass for the real thing.

words.definition: A hypocritical show of religious devotion or moral superiority.
words.example: Her sanctimony grated on us: she preached charity while ignoring the beggar at her door.
words.mnemonic: 'sancti-' (holy, as in sanctify) + '-mony' — a phony, coin-thin display of holiness.

words.definition: Marked by exaggerated or affected devotion, often making a showy display of religious feeling.
words.example: His pietistic tone—hands clasped, eyes raised—struck everyone as more performance than faith.
words.mnemonic: Think of a 'Pietà' statue posed for the camera: staged, showy holiness.

words.definition: Trickery or the use of clever, deceptive arguments to gain an unfair advantage.
words.example: The lawyer won through chicane, burying the truth under a maze of petty technicalities.
words.mnemonic: A 'chicane' is a tight S-bend on a racetrack — chicanery swerves you away from the straight truth.

words.definition: A dishonest person who falsely claims to have medical or other expert skill.
words.example: The so-called doctor was a quack, selling colored water as a cure for every disease.
words.mnemonic: A duck goes 'quack' — a fake healer just makes noise, ducking real medicine.

words.definition: A person who deceives others by pretending to be someone or something they are not.
words.example: The guard exposed the impostor when the man couldn't recall his own supposed name.
words.mnemonic: im-POST-or: someone who occupies a 'post' or position that was never really theirs.

words.definition: A person who makes a false or unproven claim, especially to a throne or rank.
words.example: When the true heir returned, the pretender who had seized the crown fled the palace.
words.mnemonic: Break it into 'pre-tend': someone who 'tends' to a throne before having any right to it.

words.definition: A person who hides their real feelings, motives, or beliefs behind a false front.
words.example: A skilled dissembler, he smiled warmly at rivals he was quietly plotting to ruin.
words.mnemonic: Read it as 'dis-assembler': he takes apart any resemblance between his true self and his mask.

words.definition: Deliberate deception carried out for unfair or unlawful gain, or a person who deceives.
words.example: Investigators charged him with fraud after he pocketed millions from fake charities.
words.mnemonic: Rhymes with 'flawed' — a flawed, dishonest scheme built to cheat people out of money.

words.definition: A cleverly made device or an artificial plan created to achieve a purpose.
words.example: The escape in the play felt like a lazy contrivance rather than an earned twist.
words.mnemonic: con + TRIVE — sounds like 'contrive'; picture a con artist tinkering together a gadget to scheme.

words.definition: Exaggeratedly emotional and sensational, appealing to the feelings rather than to reason.
words.example: She gave a melodramatic gasp and flung herself onto the couch over a broken nail.
words.mnemonic: MELODY + dramatic — a swelling violin melody plays as an actor clutches their chest.

words.definition: To invent or prepare something by mixing parts, often a story or a drink.
words.example: He concocted a wild excuse about aliens to explain why the homework vanished.
words.mnemonic: con + COOK(t) — sounds like 'cook'; picture cooking up a scheme in a bubbling pot.

words.definition: A pretentious or absurd ceremonial display that seems empty and hypocritical.
words.example: The awards gala struck him as pure mummery, all fake smiles and hollow speeches.
words.mnemonic: MUMMER + -y — imagine masked mummers wrapped like mummies parading in a silly ritual.

words.definition: Pompous, pretentious language that sounds grand but says very little.
words.example: The senator's speech was all fustian, thundering phrases that dissolved into nothing on reflection.
words.mnemonic: FUSS + tian — a lot of FUSS and puffed-up, fussy words signifying nothing.

words.definition: Boastful, inflated talk or swaggering, self-important behavior.
words.example: His endless rodomontade about conquests fooled no one at the poker table.
words.mnemonic: Rodomonte was a boastful knight of epic; picture him at a 'rodeo' shouting his own praises.

words.definition: Empty, arrogant self-praise, or a swaggering person who indulges in it.
words.example: All his pre-fight braggadocio evaporated the moment the bell actually rang.
words.mnemonic: BRAGGA-docio — sounds like 'bragger' dressed up with a fancy Italian flourish.

words.definition: To speak in a loud, aggressive, empty way, or to blow violently like wind.
words.example: He blustered about suing everyone, but never contacted a single lawyer.
words.mnemonic: BLOW + bluff = bluster; blustery wind puffing out a loudmouth's empty threats.

words.definition: Excessive, boastful pride in one's own achievements or qualities.
words.example: Driven by vainglory, the general ordered a monument to himself before the battle ended.
words.mnemonic: VAIN + GLORY — a peacock chasing empty glory while admiring its own reflection.

words.definition: Boastfully and excessively proud of oneself.
words.example: His vainglorious speech listed every award he had ever won, twice.
words.mnemonic: VAIN + GLORIOUS — someone who thinks their own 'glory' is glorious; a strutting peacock.

words.definition: Impressively grand in an exaggerated, pompous, or unrealistically ambitious way.
words.example: His grandiose plan to build a private space station never got past the napkin sketch.
words.mnemonic: GRAND + -iose — imagine a 'grand' palace so oversized it becomes absurdly pompous.

words.definition: To display something showily to attract attention and impress others.
words.example: She flaunted her new diamonds at the reunion, angling her hand under every light.
words.mnemonic: FLAUNT rhymes with 'taunt' — you flaunt to taunt, waving wealth in faces. (Don't confuse with 'flout,' to defy.)

description: advanced and low-frequency — sincerity and pretence
